demographics: Slightly more common in males overall, though the gap has narrowed as smoking patterns have converged
More common in people with lower income and less education, largely reflecting smoking and occupational exposure patterns
More common in rural areas of the US

risk_factors.text: Current or former cigarette smoking (most people with COPD have smoked)
Occupational exposure to dusts, fumes, or vapors (mining, welding, farming, construction)
Family history of COPD in a smoker
Indoor and outdoor air pollution exposure

family_history: COPD in a parent or sibling who smoked
social_history: Current or former tobacco use, often 20 or more pack-years
Exposure to secondhand smoke at home or work
Often lives in a rural area or has worked in manufacturing, mining, or farming
exposures: Wood or biomass smoke from cooking or heating

chief_complaints.text: I get short of breath when I walk or climb stairs
I've had this cough for months and it won't go away
I cough up phlegm every morning
My chest feels tight and I wheeze
I can't do the things I used to do

hpi.onset: Gradual, over months to years; often attributed to aging or being out of shape at first
hpi.duration: Chronic, usually present for years by the time of diagnosis
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; shortness of breath that once only occurred with heavy exertion now occurs with walking on flat ground or routine activities
hpi.quality: Shortness of breath with activity, a daily productive cough, and wheezing
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at first, becoming limiting; patients often describe stopping activities they used to enjoy
hpi.timing: Cough and sputum worst in the morning; breathlessness worse with exertion and during respiratory infections

associated_symptoms.text: Chronic cough, often productive of clear or white sputum
Waking at night short of breath or coughing
Weight loss and loss of muscle mass
Swelling in the ankles and feet

pertinent_negatives: Sudden severe shortness of breath at rest
New unilateral leg swelling or pain

negatives: Sudden onset of breathlessness at rest

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, speaks in full sentences, no distress
general.moderate: Mildly tachypneic with exertion, speaks in full sentences at rest, pursed-lip breathing may be seen
general.severe: Sits upright and leans forward, pursed-lip breathing, speaks in short phrases, barrel chest
general.critical: Accessory muscle use, tripod positioning, speaks in words, may be confused or drowsy

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest from the side and front
findings.finding: Increased anteroposterior diameter (barrel chest)

findings.maneuver: Auscultate and observe the respiratory cycle
findings.finding: Prolonged expiratory phase

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields during quiet and forced breathing
findings.finding: Diffuse expiratory wheezing
Diminished breath sounds, especially at the bases
Coarse crackles that may clear with cough
Hyperresonance to percussion

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's breathing at rest
findings.finding: Use of sternocleidomastoid and intercostal muscles
Pursed-lip breathing
Leaning forward with arms braced on knees or table
Clubbing is absent

findings.maneuver: Press the dorsum of each foot and the lower leg
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the ankles and feet

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips and nail beds
findings.finding: Central or peripheral cyanosis

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and level of alertness
findings.finding: Confusion, somnolence, or agitation suggesting hypercapnia

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular venous pulsation at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Jugular venous pressure is not elevated
No S3 gallop or new murmur

labs.caveat: Secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxemia; more likely with resting hypoxemia or chronic severe disease.
Anemia of chronic disease is also common and worsens dyspnea; a low hemoglobin is not explained by COPD itself.
A higher eosinophil count predicts a better response to inhaled corticosteroids.
Elevated bicarbonate is a compensatory response to chronic carbon dioxide retention; a normal bicarbonate does not exclude hypercapnia.
Measured on arterial blood gas. Chronic retention is usually compensated with a near-normal pH; a low pH indicates acute-on-chronic respiratory failure.
Measured on arterial blood gas. Rising PaCO2 with a falling pH signals impending respiratory failure and need for ventilatory support.
Measured on arterial blood gas. Hypoxemia is common in moderate to severe disease and worsens during exacerbations.
Measured on arterial blood gas; correlates with pulse oximetry but is more accurate in severe disease.
Metabolic compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis.
Mildly elevated in right heart strain from cor pulmonale; marked elevation suggests heart failure as the cause of dyspnea.
Same interpretation as BNP; useful when heart failure is in the differential.
Low values argue against bacterial pneumonia and can support withholding antibiotics during an exacerbation.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Tall peaked P waves in the inferior leads (P pulmonale)
Right axis deviation
Low-voltage QRS complexes
Right bundle branch block or incomplete right bundle branch block
Poor R wave progression across the precordial leads
ST depression or T wave inversion in the inferior leads from right heart strain
Atrial fibrillation

findings.text: Increased retrosternal air space on the lateral view
Prominent central pulmonary arteries with rapid tapering of peripheral vessels
Enlarged right ventricle or right atrial border suggesting cor pulmonale
Centrilobular or panlobular emphysema with upper-lobe predominance
Basilar-predominant emphysema suggesting alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Filling defect in a pulmonary artery (pulmonary embolism)
Emphysema and air trapping as incidental findings

imaging.preferred_when: When cor pulmonale or heart failure is suspected

findings.text: Elevated estimated right ventricular systolic pressure
Flattening of the interventricular septum in diastole

imaging.preferred_when: When pulmonary embolism is suspected and CT angiography is contraindicated

findings.text: Patchy matched defects from heterogeneous ventilation

initial.why: Looks for hyperinflation and excludes pneumonia, pneumothorax, heart failure, and masses
Screens for hypoxemia and guides the need for oxygen
Required to confirm airflow obstruction; a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms obstruction
Looks for anemia, polycythemia, and leukocytosis during an exacerbation
Assesses bicarbonate as a marker of chronic carbon dioxide retention and checks electrolytes
Assesses hypoxemia and hypercapnia in severe disease or suspected respiratory failure
initial.only_if: severe disease, suspected hypercapnia, or altered mental status

initial.why: Screens for arrhythmia, right heart strain, and ischemia
Distinguishes heart failure from COPD when the cause of dyspnea is unclear

initial.only_if: COPD before age 45, never-smoker, family history, or basilar-predominant emphysema

supporting.why: Characterizes emphysema and evaluates for bronchiectasis or lung cancer
supporting.only_if: symptoms are disproportionate to spirometry, or lung cancer or bronchiectasis is suspected

supporting.why: Assesses right ventricular function and pulmonary pressures
supporting.only_if: cor pulmonale or heart failure is suspected

supporting.why: Helps decide whether antibiotics are needed during an exacerbation

supporting.only_if: pulmonary embolism is suspected (sudden worsening dyspnea, pleuritic pain, or risk factors)
pulmonary embolism is suspected and CT angiography is contraindicated

supporting.why: Screens for pulmonary embolism in low-risk patients
supporting.only_if: pulmonary embolism is suspected and pretest probability is low

not_indicated.why: Not useful when pretest probability for pulmonary embolism is moderate or high; imaging is needed instead
Not needed to diagnose COPD when spirometry is available
Not part of routine COPD diagnosis
Not indicated unless pulmonary embolism is suspected
Not indicated unless pulmonary embolism is suspected and CT angiography is contraindicated
Not needed in mild disease with normal oxygen saturation
Not needed in a typical older smoker with upper-lobe emphysema

decision_points: Spirometry is required to confirm the diagnosis; a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow obstruction
Assess oxygen saturation and consider arterial blood gas when severe disease, hypercapnia, or altered mental status is present
Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin testing in younger patients, never-smokers, or those with a family history
Evaluate for pulmonary embolism when dyspnea worsens suddenly without another explanation
Assess for heart failure when orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or an elevated BNP is present

criteria.name: Spirometric definition of airflow obstruction
criteria.summary: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow obstruction and supports the diagnosis of COPD in a patient with compatible symptoms and exposure history. Severity is graded by the post-bronchodilator FEV1 percent predicted.

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Wheezing, cough, and episodic breathlessness in a patient with airflow obstruction

history: Symptoms began in childhood or young adulthood
Symptoms are episodic and variable rather than daily and progressive
Symptoms triggered by allergens, exercise, or cold air
Often has allergic rhinitis or eczema
labs: Fractional exhaled nitric oxide is often elevated
imaging: Chest x-ray is usually normal without hyperinflation

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and leg swelling in an older patient with a smoking history
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or elevated jugular venous pressure

history: Orthopnea and waking at night short of breath
Rapid weight gain with swelling
Known coronary disease or hypertension
exam: Bibasilar crackles that do not clear with cough
imaging: Cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, or pleural effusions on chest x-ray
Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction on echocardiogram

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Productive cough, fever, and breathlessness in a patient with chronic lung disease

history: Acute onset over days rather than years
Fever, chills, and pleuritic chest pain
exam: Focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds
Dullness to percussion over one area
imaging: Focal consolidation or infiltrate on chest x-ray

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden worsening of breathlessness in a patient with chronic lung disease
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, or hypoxemia out of proportion to exam

history: Sudden onset rather than gradual worsening
Pleuritic chest pain
Recent immobility, surgery, or long travel
Prior venous thromboembolism
exam: Unilateral leg swelling or calf tenderness
labs: Elevated D-dimer in low pretest probability
imaging: Filling defect in a pulmonary artery on CT angiography
Mismatched segmental perfusion defects on ventilation-perfusion scan

differential.name: Lung cancer
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, weight loss, and a long smoking history
differential.trigger: Hemoptysis, unintentional weight loss, or a new focal finding on chest imaging

history: Hemoptysis
Unintentional weight loss
Hoarseness or new focal chest pain
exam: Focal wheeze that does not clear with cough
imaging: Solitary pulmonary nodule, mass, or hilar adenopathy on chest x-ray or CT

differential.name: Bronchiectasis
differential.why_considered: Chronic productive cough with daily sputum in a patient with airflow obstruction

history: Large volumes of purulent sputum daily
Recurrent respiratory infections
History of severe childhood pneumonia
exam: Coarse crackles that change with coughing
imaging: Dilated airways with a signet-ring appearance and tram-track lines on high-resolution CT

differential.name: Tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats in a patient with abnormal chest imaging

history: Night sweats and fever
Weight loss
Immigration from or travel to a high-prevalence country
Incarceration or shelter residence
labs: Positive interferon-gamma release assay or acid-fast bacilli on sputum
imaging: Upper-lobe cavitary lesions or apical infiltrates on chest x-ray

severity.mild: Symptoms with heavy exertion only; post-bronchodilator FEV1 at or above 80% predicted; oxygen saturation normal at rest; no exacerbations in the past year
severity.moderate: Daily dyspnea with routine activity; FEV1 50 to 79% predicted; occasional exacerbations requiring bronchodilators or oral steroids; oxygen saturation 90 to 95% at rest
severity.severe: Dyspnea with minimal activity; FEV1 30 to 49% predicted; frequent exacerbations; resting hypoxemia or chronic carbon dioxide retention; barrel chest and accessory muscle use
severity.critical: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 50 mmHg; altered mental status; oxygen saturation below 88% despite supplemental oxygen; may require noninvasive or invasive ventilation

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status, somnolence, or agitation
red_flags.meaning: Hypercapnic encephalopathy; impending respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support

red_flags.finding: Respiratory rate above 30 or use of accessory muscles at rest
red_flags.meaning: Respiratory distress; needs urgent assessment and likely admission

red_flags.finding: Oxygen saturation below 88% on room air or falling despite oxygen
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; evaluate for exacerbation, pneumonia, or pulmonary embolism
Evaluate for lung cancer, bronchiectasis, or pulmonary embolism

red_flags.finding: Sudden onset of pleuritic chest pain with unilateral leg swelling
New unilateral absent breath sounds with hyperresonance and hypotension
red_flags.meaning: Pneumothorax, which is more common in emphysema and can be life-threatening

red_flags.finding: Fever with focal crackles and leukocytosis
red_flags.meaning: Infectious exacerbation or pneumonia requiring antibiotics

complications.name: Acute exacerbation of COPD
clues: Increased dyspnea, cough, and sputum over days
Worsening hypoxemia
Often triggered by viral or bacterial respiratory infection

complications.name: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure
clues: Drowsiness or confusion
Rising PaCO2 with falling pH on arterial blood gas
Accessory muscle use and inability to speak in full sentences

complications.name: Cor pulmonale and right heart failure
clues: Peripheral edema
Elevated jugular venous pressure
Right ventricular dilation or elevated pulmonary pressures on echocardiogram

complications.name: Secondary polycythemia
clues: Elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit
Chronic resting hypoxemia
Increased blood viscosity symptoms such as headache

complications.name: Pneumothorax
clues: Sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea
Absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side
More common with bullous emphysema

complications.name: Lung cancer
clues: Hemoptysis
Unintentional weight loss
New focal findings on chest imaging

complications.name: Depression and anxiety
clues: Low mood, loss of interest, or persistent worry about breathing
Social withdrawal and reduced activity

complications.name: Osteoporosis
clues: Fragility fracture
Long-term inhaled or systemic corticosteroid use
Low bone mineral density on DXA

special_populations.differences: Symptoms may be attributed to normal aging or deconditioning; comorbid heart failure and coronary disease are common and can mimic or worsen dyspnea; polypharmacy and cognitive impairment affect inhaler technique.

Dyspnea is common in normal pregnancy, so worsening symptoms need objective assessment; smoking cessation is the highest-yield intervention; maintain oxygen saturation above 95% to protect fetal oxygenation.
Obesity worsens dyspnea and exercise limitation and can reduce functional status independent of lung function; weight loss and pulmonary rehabilitation improve symptoms.
Systemic corticosteroids used for exacerbations can cause marked hyperglycemia; monitor glucose closely and use the lowest effective steroid dose.

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or have you ever smoked? How much and for how many years?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former cigarette use with a substantial pack-year burden; quantifies the main risk factor

key_questions.question: When did you quit, if you have quit?
key_questions.looking_for: Former smoker; ongoing risk persists after quitting

key_questions.question: How long have you been short of breath, and what brings it on now compared with a year ago?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual, progressive dyspnea over months to years, now with less exertion than before

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough? Is it dry or do you bring up phlegm?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic productive cough, often worst in the morning

key_questions.question: Do you wheeze or feel tightness in your chest?
What activities can you no longer do because of your breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Functional limitation; gauges severity and impact on daily life

key_questions.question: Have you had flare-ups where your breathing got much worse, and did you need steroids, antibiotics, or a hospital visit?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior exacerbations, which predict future exacerbations and guide treatment

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have asthma, or used an inhaler?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing asthma or prior inhaler use; asthma is a risk factor and a look-alike

key_questions.question: Have you been exposed to dusts, fumes, or chemicals at work, or to secondhand smoke?
Do you wake at night short of breath, or need extra pillows to sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in typical COPD; present suggests heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you coughed up blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Hemoptysis, which raises concern for lung cancer, bronchiectasis, or pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss, which raises concern for lung cancer or advanced disease

key_questions.question: Have you had sudden severe shortness of breath or sharp chest pain with a swollen leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Features suggesting pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have COPD or emphysema, or did you develop lung problems at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history or early onset raising concern for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

key_questions.question: How much does your breathing affect your mood or your ability to get around?

reasoning_points: Gradual, progressive exertional dyspnea over months to years in a patient with a substantial smoking history
Risk factors such as smoking, occupational dust or fume exposure, or long-standing asthma
Exam findings of prolonged expiration, diffuse wheezing, hyperresonance, and possibly barrel chest
Spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirming persistent airflow obstruction
Chest imaging with hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms, and exclusion of look-alikes such as heart failure, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and lung cancer

easy: Older adult with a long smoking history
Years of progressive exertional dyspnea with a daily productive cough
Prolonged expiration and diffuse wheezing on exam
Hyperinflated chest x-ray with flattened diaphragms
medium: Dyspnea attributed to aging or being out of shape
Coexisting heart failure or obesity confusing the picture
Normal chest x-ray with only spirometry confirming the diagnosis
Chronic carbon dioxide retention with a near-normal pH and elevated bicarbonate
hard: Younger patient or never-smoker raising concern for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Sudden worsening dyspnea from pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax rather than a simple exacerbation
Severe disease with hypercapnic encephalopathy and impending respiratory failure
Hemoptysis or weight loss suggesting coexisting lung cancer
